cards.statement: The docs suggest a full 40-character SHA as the `include:project` ref for the most stable result.
cards.explanation: A short SHA can be ambiguous, while the full SHA ensures GitLab reads the intended commit. A fully qualified ref such as refs/tags/<tag> is the other suggested option.

cards.statement: An `include` placed at the bottom of `.gitlab-ci.yml` lets included keys override the file's own keys.
cards.explanation: GitLab evaluates included files first wherever the include keyword appears, so values in .gitlab-ci.yml take precedence over included ones.
cards.misconception: The position of include in the file decides which configuration wins.

cards.statement: A job in `.gitlab-ci.yml` that reuses an included job's name discards that included job's other keys.
cards.explanation: GitLab merges same-named jobs from included files and .gitlab-ci.yml, so keys the local job leaves unset keep their included values.
cards.misconception: Redefining an included job replaces the whole included definition.

source.title: Use CI/CD configuration from other files

cards.statement: Retrying a single job after an included file changes makes GitLab fetch that included file again.
cards.explanation: A retried job uses the configuration GitLab fetched when it created the pipeline. A new pipeline fetches the included files again and picks up changes.
cards.misconception: Job retries pick up changes made to included files.

cards.statement: A nested `include:local` in a file from another project resolves its path in that other project.
cards.explanation: GitLab evaluates include based on the location of the file that contains it, not the project running the pipeline.

cards.statement: For a private `include:project` source, the pipeline user needs at least the Reporter role in that project.
cards.explanation: With a lower role, GitLab shows a not found or access denied error. Internal projects accept any authenticated non-external user and public projects need no membership.

cards.statement: `include:remote` can fetch a YAML file from a private URL that requires HTTP authentication to read.
cards.explanation: include:remote takes a public URL reachable with an HTTP or HTTPS GET request and supports no authentication. For a private project on the same instance, use include:project.
cards.misconception: include:remote can authenticate to the URL it fetches.

cards.statement: With `include:integrity`, GitLab fails the pipeline when the remote file's SHA256 hash differs from the given one.
cards.explanation: include:integrity takes a Base64-encoded SHA256 hash of an include:remote file. On a mismatch GitLab does not process the file, which guards against changed remote content.

cards.statement: With `extends`, a job's own `script` array replaces the template's `script` instead of adding to it.
cards.explanation: extends deep-merges hashes such as variables but replaces arrays such as script and tags with the value from the last member.

cards.statement: A job using `extends` still inherits the template's `variables` when it sets its own `variables: null`.
cards.explanation: Assigning null to a key in a job that uses extends excludes that key from the extended content, so the job keeps none of the template's variables.
cards.misconception: The extends merge ignores a null value, so the inherited hash stays.

cards.statement: A YAML alias in `.gitlab-ci.yml` can reuse an anchor defined in a file added with `include`.
cards.explanation: YAML anchors are valid in the file that defines them. To reuse configuration from another file, use extends or !reference tags.
cards.misconception: YAML anchors work across files combined with include.

cards.statement: A job can build its `rules` array from several `!reference` tags that point at rule lists elsewhere.
cards.explanation: GitLab combines the referenced lists into one rules array. Building an array this way works for rules, script and stages; other keywords give a validation error.

cards.statement: A component can be a `templates/<name>/` directory, whose `template.yml` is the one file other projects use.
cards.explanation: Other files in that directory, such as tests or a Dockerfile, are not released with the component. A single templates/<name>.yml file is the alternative layout.

cards.statement: Each component in a component project gets its own version, independent of the project's other components.
cards.explanation: All components in a component project are versioned together. A component that needs different versioning belongs in a dedicated component project.
cards.misconception: Components in one project are versioned separately.

cards.statement: On GitLab Self-Managed, `include:component` can load a component straight from GitLab.com.
cards.explanation: include:component references components on the same GitLab instance as the project. To use a GitLab.com component on GitLab Self-Managed, mirror its project there (Premium and Ultimate).
cards.misconception: Components can be included across GitLab instances.

cards.statement: If a commit SHA and a tag share a name, `include:component` uses the commit SHA as the version.
cards.explanation: Version resolution ranks a commit SHA above a tag and a tag above a branch of the same name, then ~latest or partial versions from the CI/CD Catalog.

cards.statement: `~latest` in `include:component` picks a pre-release like `2.0.0-rc` when it is the newest published version.
cards.explanation: ~latest and partial versions skip pre-releases, which GitLab does not treat as production-ready. To use one, reference its full version, such as 2.0.0-rc.

cards.statement: Publishing a component version to the CI/CD Catalog requires a CI/CD job that uses the `release` keyword.
cards.explanation: The catalog accepts releases created by the release keyword in a job, not through the Releases API, typically in a pipeline for a semantic version tag.

cards.statement: `spec:inputs` belongs in a header that a `---` line separates from the rest of the configuration file.
cards.explanation: spec is a header keyword declared at the top of the file. When the file also defines jobs, the --- YAML document separator ends the header.

cards.statement: An input in `spec:inputs` that omits `default` is optional for configurations that include the file.
cards.explanation: Inputs are mandatory unless spec:inputs:default sets a default value, so each include of the file must set them under include:inputs.

cards.statement: Input values stay fixed for the whole pipeline once GitLab interpolates them at pipeline creation.
cards.explanation: GitLab interpolates $[[ inputs.* ]] when it fetches the configuration. Unlike CI/CD variables, nothing a job does during the pipeline can change them.

cards.statement: An input that omits `spec:inputs:type` accepts any YAML value, including arrays and booleans.
cards.explanation: Inputs expect strings unless spec:inputs:type sets array, number or boolean.
cards.misconception: Untyped inputs accept any value type.

cards.statement: Since GitLab 19.0, `options` can restrict which values an `array` type input accepts.
cards.explanation: The pipeline fails to start if any item of the array input is missing from the options list. A manual run shows the options as a multi-select list.

cards.statement: A file added with `include` can read the inputs defined in the file that includes it.
cards.explanation: Input values are available in the file whose spec section defines them. To use a value in an included file, pass it explicitly with include:inputs.
cards.misconception: Included files inherit the including file's inputs.
